name: Chicken Wing Defense
summary: The chicken wing is the position you end up in when a ball is driven at the shoulder of your paddle arm: the elbow lifts, the wrist collapses, and whatever comes off the paddle floats. Good players aim there on purpose. The defence is footwork and paddle position, not a stronger arm.
whenToUse: A speed-up is coming at your dominant-side shoulder or hip.
You are at the kitchen line with no time to step around the ball.
The opponents have worked out where your awkward spot is and keep going back to it.
You are in a hands battle and the exchange is arriving at your body.
howTo: Start with the paddle up and slightly toward your dominant shoulder — most body balls arrive there.
Take the ball with a backhand, not a forehand, whenever it is inside your shoulder line.
Move your feet away from the ball rather than folding your arm around it: a small step opens the whole shot up.
Keep the elbow down and in front, and let the paddle face do the blocking.
Absorb rather than counter — the goal is a ball that dies in their kitchen.
Reset the paddle to the middle before the next one arrives.
commonMistakes: Turning it into a forehand, which is what raises the elbow in the first place.
Standing still and reaching, so the contact point ends up behind the shoulder.
Trying to counter hard out of a cramped position, which floats the ball up.
Holding the paddle low at rest, which means it has to travel up and across.
Blaming the shot rather than the position — this is a footwork problem.

drills.name: Body bag
drills.description: Your partner speeds up deliberately at your paddle-side shoulder, over and over. Block every one with a backhand. No forehands allowed however tempting.

drills.name: One step out
drills.description: Same feed, but you must take one small step away from the ball before every block. It proves how much room a single step buys.
